catalog_quote: One part of each Narak word is said on a higher pitch or tone. When this higher pitch consists of a high pitch on the final syllable which then glides down, or one that goes up on the second-last syllable and glides down on the last syllable, it has an acute mark on the highest pitched syllable. The written form of many Narak words are distinguished only by an acute marking the tone difference. [p. 17] ... When there is an acute mark it is always on the last or second-last syllable, and there is never more than one acute on a word. [p. 18] ... There are four (4) different word tone patterns: 1. High-Level: The last syllable is a little higher than all previous syllables in the word ... This is the most frequent pattern. 2. Upglide: The last syllable has a tone which glides up. ... 3. Downglide (on last syllable): The last syllable is higher than the preceding ones, and then glides down ... 4. High Pitch (on second-last syllable), then downglide (on last syllable) [pp. 18-19] ... Each of them consists of a Grammatical word, which has a specific word tone pattern. The contrastive pitch only occurs on the last two syllables, any preceding syllables are said on a lower pitch. When a suffix is attached the tone moves towards the end of the word. [p. 30]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Narak is described as a word-tone language, not a stress language: each (grammatical) word carries exactly one tonal peak, and contrastive pitch is confined to the last two syllables. Four word-tone patterns are distinguished — (1) final high-level (unmarked, most frequent), (2) final upglide (unmarked; asterisk in the dictionary), (3) final high-falling downglide (acute on the final syllable), (4) high on the penult then falling on the final (acute on the penult) — plus a mid-falling tone on clitics. The OPD (Hainsworth 1992/2004, p. 3) states the same as 'four distinct contrasting tones.. Only the last two syllables of the word carry the contrastive tone pattern'. Neither source says anything about stress; the pronunciation guide only says acute vowels are said 'on a higher or stronger pitch'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned (no stress statement at all).
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics (hyphenated) lie outside the tone-bearing word and take their own mid-falling tone without perturbing the host; suffixes move the tone rightward (ápo 'grandmother' > apóna 'my grandmother'); negative and imperative verb forms always take descending tone; a syllabic n or w may carry the tone where a vowel has been lost (na.ń.no 'I will not eat'); loanwords from English/Tok Pisin are often said with descending tone and may not follow the native rules (éytiy 'eighty'); the final upglide is suppressed before a clitic and on the first of two adjacent upglide words.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word = grammatical word plus any hyphenated clitics; the tone pattern belongs to the grammatical word (citation/dictionary headword forms). Statement is orthography-oriented, based on ~50 years of SIL fieldwork at Amboka/Tabibuga; no instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary and OPD describe the Narak of the Tabibuga / Amboka area of the middle Jimi valley (Wurm's 'Narak' proper, the SIL variety). Kandawo (Wurm's 'Gandja', ISO gam) is treated by Glottolog as a separate language under the Kandawo-Narak node kand1306; Wurm 1975:517-518 regarded the two as aberrant dialects of one language. No dialect split is claimed for the tone description.

new_statements.quote: "The last syllable or syllables of a word carry the contrastive tone pattern and the rest of the word has a level non-contrastive phonetically Low tone" [p. 5]; "it seems that the basic tonal contrast of Narak is minimally a High tone vs. a High-Falling tone. If the High-Falling tone is on a monosyllabic word, it surfaces as simply a Falling tone, but in polysyllabic words, the High surfaces on the penultimate syllable and the Falling on the final one. A Low tone fills in any preceding syllables. Similarly, for a High-toned word, the High is on the rightmost syllable, and any previous syllables have a Low tone." [p. 6]

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement (Hainsworth et al. 2019/2021 dictionary: word tone, contrastive pitch confined to the last two syllables, acute never left of the penult) — so it agrees on 'tone language, no stress statement' — and adds the phonological abstraction (H vs. HF melodies, default Low fill, penult-H + final-F for the falling type, toneless suffixes, allotonic rising contours) from Hainsworth's 1969 manuscript. The catalog record itself has an empty rule field; nothing in Cahill supports a stress rule for it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Narak is treated as a word-tone language, not a stress language: the word 'stress' is never applied to Narak (Cahill lists other PNG languages with predictable or contrastive stress on p. 4 and Narak is not among them). Each word carries one of two basic tone patterns, H or HF, realised on the last syllable(s): H on the rightmost syllable (LH, LLH) or H on the penult plus Falling on the final (HF, LHF); all preceding syllables get a default Low. Cahill classes it as 'slightly different' from both word-tone subtypes (melody spreading vs. tone on one stressed/nuclear syllable), p. 5. Noun suffixes add no tone of their own ('the noun stem contributes the tone, and the suffix makes no contribution', p. 6; contrast with Kairi on p. 8). Data are reproduced from Hainsworth 1969 'Narak word tone' (unpublished ms.).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress analysis at all).
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 1 (p. 6): Rising and Rising-Falling tone patterns are attested but 'quite limited' and treated as allotones; Rising occurs on monosyllables with sonorant codas [m, n, j, w] and vowel [a, e, o] (allotone of High); Rising-Falling in forms like 'I will eat' arises from medial-vowel elision leaving the LHF pattern behind. p. 19: Narak among languages that 'seem to require a High tone in a word'.
new_statements.identity_note: Cahill's data are Narak as recorded by Joan Hainsworth (SIL, Jimi Valley / Western Highlands); no dialect is named. Cahill's section 2.1 is a secondary summary of Hainsworth 1969 'Narak word tone' (manuscript), not primary fieldwork.

sources.note: Front matter 'Phonology and Spelling' (pp. 16-37) describes Narak as a word-tone language: one tonal peak per word, contrastive pitch only on the last two syllables, four word-tone patterns plus a mid-falling clitic tone; suffixes shift the tone rightward, clitics do not. The word 'stress' is never used; acute vowels are 'said on a higher or stronger pitch' (p. 22).
